source.title: Why We Sleep
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of Why We Sleep by Matthew Walker (2017). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright.

cards.title: Go to bed and wake up at the same time, weekends included
cards.body:
Walker's most repeated piece of advice is consistency. Your body runs on an internal daily clock, and a regular bedtime and wake time help it know when to make you sleepy and when to make you alert. Sleeping in late at weekends and then rising early on Monday shifts that clock back and forth, a bit like mild jet lag.

A steady schedule is one of the simplest, most widely recommended habits for better sleep. If sleep problems persist despite good habits, see a doctor.
cards.apply_it: Set a fixed wake-up time for the next seven days, including the weekend, and keep to it even after a poor night.

quiz.question: Why does Walker stress a consistent sleep schedule?
options: It helps your internal body clock regulate sleepiness and alertness
It lets you need less sleep
It only matters for children
It replaces the need for darkness
quiz.explanation: Regular timing supports the body's daily rhythm, making sleep easier.

cards.title: Bright light in the morning, dim light in the evening
cards.body:
Light is the main signal that sets your body clock. Walker explains that bright light, and especially the blue-rich light from screens and LEDs, in the evening can delay the release of melatonin, the hormone that helps signal that it's night. That can make it harder to fall asleep.

The flip side is that daylight earlier in the day helps anchor your rhythm. Dimming lights and putting devices away in the hour before bed is a simple, low-cost change.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, dim the lights and put your phone out of reach for the last hour before bed. Tomorrow, get some daylight soon after waking.

quiz.question: How can evening light, including from screens, affect sleep?
options: It makes melatonin work faster
It can delay melatonin and make falling asleep harder
It has no effect
It deepens sleep
quiz.explanation: Light signals daytime to the body clock, pushing back the cues for sleep.

cards.title: Caffeine lingers for hours, and alcohol makes sleep worse, not better
cards.body:
Walker points out that caffeine stays in your system for many hours, so an afternoon coffee can still be acting at bedtime, blocking the build-up of sleepiness even if you manage to drop off.

Alcohol is often mistaken for a sleep aid. It can make you drowsy, but it's a sedative rather than natural sleep: it tends to fragment the night with brief awakenings and reduces REM sleep, the stage linked with dreaming. Cutting back on both, especially later in the day, is mainstream advice.
cards.apply_it: Set a caffeine cut-off around midday for a week and avoid alcohol close to bedtime. Notice how you feel in the mornings.

quiz.question: What does Walker say about alcohol and sleep?
options: It improves sleep quality
It only affects dreams positively
It may cause drowsiness but fragments sleep and reduces REM
It has no effect on sleep
quiz.explanation: Sedation is not the same as healthy sleep; alcohol disrupts its structure.

cards.title: Keep the bedroom cool and dark
cards.body:
To fall asleep, your core body temperature needs to drop a little. Walker explains that a cool bedroom helps that happen, while a warm, stuffy room works against it. A warm bath before bed can also help, because it draws heat to the skin and you cool down afterwards.

Darkness matters too, so blackout curtains or an eye mask can help. If you lie awake for a long time, getting up and doing something calm until you feel sleepy is better than tossing and turning. If insomnia continues, talk to a doctor.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, make your bedroom a little cooler and darker than usual, and move any glowing devices out of sight.

quiz.question: Why does a cool bedroom help sleep?
options: Cold makes you dream more
Warm rooms improve melatonin
Temperature doesn't matter
The body needs to lower its core temperature to fall asleep
quiz.explanation: A drop in core temperature is part of the body's process for falling asleep.

cards.title: Sleep helps lock in what you learned during the day
cards.body:
Walker draws on research showing that sleep plays a role in memory. Sleep before learning seems to help prepare the brain to take in new information, and sleep after learning helps strengthen and store it, so it is less likely to be lost.

This is a strong argument against all-nighters before exams or presentations. Cutting sleep to study more can undercut the very learning you're trying to do. Spreading study over several days, with proper nights in between, tends to work better.
cards.apply_it: If you have something important to learn this week, study it in shorter sessions across several days and protect a full night's sleep before the big day.

quiz.question: What role does sleep play in learning, according to Walker?
options: It helps prepare the brain to learn and strengthens memories afterwards
It erases what you studied
It only matters for physical skills
None, if you study hard enough
quiz.explanation: Sleep supports both taking in new information and consolidating it.

cards.title: Two forces decide when you feel sleepy
cards.body:
Walker explains that two systems work together to time your sleep. One is your internal 24-hour clock, which raises and lowers alertness across the day. The other is sleep pressure: a chemical called adenosine builds up in the brain the longer you stay awake, making you steadily drowsier until sleep clears it away.

When the two line up, falling asleep is easy. When they clash, for example after a long late nap or a night flight, you can feel wired at bedtime or groggy at noon. Knowing both helps explain why timing matters as much as total hours.
cards.apply_it: Notice when you feel sleepiest today, and ask whether it's your body clock, a long stretch awake, or both.

quiz.question: According to Walker, what builds up in the brain the longer you stay awake?
options: Melatonin, released by bright daylight
Caffeine, produced naturally by the body
Adenosine, which creates sleep pressure
Adrenaline, which calms the mind
quiz.explanation: Adenosine accumulates during waking hours and creates the pressure to sleep.

cards.title: Night owls and morning larks are partly built in
cards.body:
Walker describes chronotypes: some people's body clocks run early and others run late, and genes play a substantial part in which you are. A night owl forced into a very early schedule isn't lazy; they are being asked to perform near their biological low point.

Where you have some flexibility, put demanding work in your sharper hours, and be slower to judge a family member or colleague whose rhythm differs from yours. Owls still benefit from consistent timing and morning light, but they can't simply choose to become larks.
cards.apply_it: Decide whether you lean lark or owl, and move one demanding task to the time of day you usually feel sharpest.

quiz.question: How does Walker describe being a night owl?
options: A sign of laziness or poor discipline
A habit anyone can drop in a day
Something that only affects children
Largely a biological trait influenced by genes
quiz.explanation: Chronotype is substantially inherited, so owls aren't simply lazy.

cards.title: Teenagers' body clocks really do run later
cards.body:
Walker explains that during adolescence the body clock shifts later, so many teenagers genuinely don't feel sleepy until late and struggle to wake early. Very early starts can leave them chronically short of sleep. He supports later school start times, a position also taken by major paediatric organisations.

For parents, this reframes the 'lazy teenager'. Protecting a teen's sleep, with regular times, fewer late-night screens and realistic mornings, may do more for their mood, learning and safety than nagging does.
cards.apply_it: If you live with a teenager, agree together on one change, such as phones charging outside the bedroom, that would protect their sleep.

quiz.question: Why do many teenagers struggle with early mornings, according to Walker?
options: Their body clock shifts later during adolescence
They need less sleep than adults
They are simply lazy
Morning light keeps them awake
quiz.explanation: The adolescent body clock runs later, so early starts clash with their biology.

cards.title: Cutting sleep short at the end costs you the most dreaming sleep
cards.body:
Sleep moves through cycles of roughly 90 minutes, alternating between non-REM sleep and REM, or dreaming, sleep. Walker explains that the mix changes across the night: deep non-REM sleep dominates the early cycles, while REM sleep is concentrated in the last hours before morning.

So if you usually need eight hours but set an alarm two hours early, you don't lose sleep evenly; you lose a disproportionate share of your REM sleep. Both stages do important work, which is why Walker cares about the full night, not just most of it.
cards.apply_it: Look at your wake-up time. If you routinely cut the night short, try moving bedtime earlier rather than squeezing the morning.

quiz.question: Which sleep stage is concentrated in the final hours before waking?
options: Deep non-REM sleep
REM (dreaming) sleep
Light dozing only
No particular stage
quiz.explanation: REM dominates the later cycles, so an early alarm cuts into it heavily.

cards.title: Sleep before learning, not just after it
cards.body:
Walker argues that sleep doesn't only lock in memories afterwards; it also prepares the brain to take in new information. He describes studies in which sleep-deprived people formed new memories noticeably less well than rested people did. In his view, the all-nighter before an exam undermines the very learning it is meant to cram in.

Students and professionals can treat a full night's sleep as part of their preparation, not a break from it. Spreading study across several days, with sleep in between, usually works better than one long late session.
cards.apply_it: Before your next exam or big presentation, plan your preparation so you can still get a full night's sleep the night before.

quiz.question: What does Walker say about staying up all night to study?
options: It is the best way to remember facts
It only affects physical skills
It weakens the brain's ability to take in new memories
It has no effect if you drink coffee
quiz.explanation: Sleep loss impairs the brain's capacity to form new memories.

cards.title: Practise, then sleep, to sharpen a physical skill
cards.body:
Walker describes research in which people learning a motor task, such as typing a finger sequence, performed better after a night's sleep than after the same amount of time spent awake. Sleep appears to help refine and automate skills the body has practised.

Musicians, athletes and anyone learning a craft can use this. Practice still does the heavy lifting, but a good night afterwards seems to help the skill settle in. Cutting sleep to squeeze in extra practice may cost more than it gains.
cards.apply_it: When you're learning a physical skill, plan practice on days when you can protect the following night's sleep.

quiz.question: What happened in the motor-skill studies Walker describes?
options: Performance only improved after coffee
Sleep made no difference at all
Skills were forgotten after sleep
Performance improved after sleep, compared with the same time awake
quiz.explanation: Sleep after practice was linked to better performance than an equal time awake.

cards.title: Sleep on a hard problem
cards.body:
Walker describes REM sleep as a time when the brain links ideas that don't seem connected while we're awake. He cites experiments in which people were more likely to spot a hidden shortcut or solve puzzles after sleep, and argues that dreaming supports creative problem-solving.

The old advice to 'sleep on it' has some support. When a decision or creative problem is stuck, a night's rest may bring a fresh angle, which is often more useful than pushing on late into the night with a tired mind.
cards.apply_it: Write down a problem you're stuck on before bed tonight, then look at it fresh tomorrow morning before checking your phone.

quiz.question: What does Walker suggest REM sleep helps with?
options: Connecting distant ideas, which aids creative problem-solving
Burning fat
Growing taller
Erasing all memories of the day
quiz.explanation: He presents REM sleep as a time when the brain makes unusual connections.

cards.title: Dreaming may help take the sting out of painful memories
cards.body:
One of Walker's more striking ideas is that REM sleep acts like a kind of overnight therapy: the brain revisits emotional experiences in a calmer chemical state, which may soften their painful edge while keeping the lesson. He links this to research on nightmares in post-traumatic stress.

This is an interesting theory that is still being studied, not settled fact. The practical point is more modest: upsets often feel more manageable after a good night's sleep, so emotional decisions made at 2am deserve a second look in daylight.
cards.apply_it: Next time something upsets you late in the evening, write it down and agree with yourself to decide what to do after you've slept.

quiz.question: How should Walker's idea of dreaming as 'overnight therapy' be treated?
options: As proven medical fact
As an interesting theory that is still being researched
As a reason to skip therapy
As a claim that dreams predict the future
quiz.explanation: The idea is intriguing but not settled science.

cards.title: A tired brain overreacts emotionally
cards.body:
Walker describes brain-scan research from his lab in which sleep-deprived people showed a much stronger response in the amygdala, a region involved in emotional reactions, along with a weaker link to the frontal areas that help keep those reactions in check.

In daily life this fits a familiar pattern: after a short night we snap more easily, take things personally and swing between moods. Recognising that tiredness is amplifying your feelings lets you pause before a harsh reply or a big decision.
cards.apply_it: After a poor night, warn yourself in advance that you'll be more reactive, and postpone a difficult conversation if you can.

quiz.question: According to Walker, what happens to emotional reactions after sleep loss?
options: They disappear completely
They become calmer and wiser
They get stronger and harder to regulate
They are unaffected
quiz.explanation: Sleep deprivation amplified the brain's emotional response and weakened control.

cards.title: When you're short of sleep, you can't judge how impaired you are
cards.body:
Walker cites research in which people limited to about six hours a night for two weeks steadily declined on attention tests, yet rated themselves as only a little sleepy. Their performance slipped much further than they realised.

This is the hidden danger of chronic short sleep: you get used to feeling tired and assume you're fine. If others notice more mistakes, or you need caffeine just to function, those are better signals than your own sense of how you're doing.
cards.apply_it: For one week, note mistakes and lapses alongside how many hours you slept, and see whether a pattern appears.

quiz.question: What did the six-hours-a-night studies Walker cites find?
options: Six hours was enough for everyone
Performance improved over time
People felt far worse than they performed
People underestimated how much their performance had declined
quiz.explanation: Performance dropped steadily while people felt only mildly sleepy.

cards.title: Never drive when you're drowsy
cards.body:
Walker stresses that tired drivers can slip into microsleeps: brief lapses of a few seconds in which the brain disengages, often without the driver noticing. At road speed, a few seconds is enough to drift across a lane.

Opening a window or turning up the radio doesn't reliably fix it. If you're struggling to keep your eyes open, the safe options are to stop somewhere safe, take a short nap or hand over the wheel. The same caution applies to operating machinery at work.
cards.apply_it: Make a rule now: if you yawn repeatedly or drift in your lane, you pull over at the next safe place.

quiz.question: What are microsleeps?
options: Brief lapses of a few seconds in which the brain disengages
Short naps taken on purpose
Dreams you remember clearly
A type of deep sleep at night
quiz.explanation: Microsleeps are short, often unnoticed lapses that are dangerous at the wheel.

cards.title: Short sleep can push you to eat more
cards.body:
Walker describes studies suggesting that when people are short of sleep, the hormones that govern hunger and fullness shift: the signal that you've had enough tends to fall and hunger signals rise. In lab studies, sleep-restricted volunteers also ate more and reached for sugary, high-calorie snacks.

Much of this research uses small lab studies, so how big the effect is in everyday life is debated. Still, if you raid the snack cupboard after a late night, tiredness may be part of the reason, and better sleep is a sensible support for healthier eating.
cards.apply_it: Next time you crave sugary snacks, ask yourself how you slept last night before blaming your willpower.

quiz.question: What do the studies Walker describes suggest happens to appetite with short sleep?
options: Appetite disappears completely
Hunger signals tend to rise and fullness signals fall
Only cravings for vegetables increase
Nothing changes
quiz.explanation: Short sleep was linked to hormonal shifts that increase hunger, though effect sizes are debated.

cards.title: Sleep supports your body's defences
cards.body:
Walker describes research linking sleep and the immune system, including studies in which people who slept less around the time of a vaccination produced a weaker antibody response, and studies in which short sleepers were more likely to catch a cold after exposure to a virus.

Some of his broader claims about sleep and disease go further than the evidence supports, but the basic link is well established: sleep is part of how the body maintains its defences. Prioritising rest when you feel run down is a sensible, low-risk habit.
cards.apply_it: When you feel run down, treat an early night as part of looking after yourself rather than as a luxury.

quiz.question: Which finding about sleep and immunity does Walker describe?
options: Sleep has no link to immunity
Less sleep makes vaccines work better
Short sleep around a vaccination was linked to a weaker antibody response
Only children's immunity depends on sleep
quiz.explanation: Studies tied shorter sleep to weaker vaccine responses and more colds.

cards.title: You can't stockpile sleep or fully repay it at the weekend
cards.body:
Walker argues that sleep doesn't work like a bank account. You can't store it up in advance before a busy week, and sleeping in at the weekend doesn't fully make up for several short nights; the brain doesn't get back everything it missed.

That's why he puts the emphasis on enough sleep, regularly, rather than cycles of running short and catching up. An occasional late night won't ruin you, but a routine of short weeknights and long Saturday lie-ins is a poor substitute for steady rest.
cards.apply_it: Instead of planning a weekend lie-in, try going to bed 30 minutes earlier on three weeknights.

quiz.question: What does Walker say about 'catching up' on sleep?
options: A long weekend lie-in fully resets you
You can store sleep for busy weeks
Missing sleep has no lasting effect
Sleep can't be stockpiled, and catch-up doesn't fully repay a deficit
quiz.explanation: He stresses regular sufficient sleep over cycles of deprivation and recovery.

cards.title: If you nap, keep it early and short
cards.body:
Many people feel a natural dip in alertness in the early afternoon, and Walker notes that a short nap can restore alertness. But a nap also releases some of the sleep pressure you need to fall asleep at night.

His advice is to avoid napping late in the afternoon, roughly after 3pm, and if you struggle to sleep at night, to drop naps altogether. A brief rest after lunch suits some people; a long nap at 5pm often means lying awake at midnight.
cards.apply_it: If you nap, set an alarm so it stays short and finish before mid-afternoon. If nights are hard, try a week with no naps.

quiz.question: Why does Walker warn against late-afternoon naps?
options: They release sleep pressure you need to fall asleep at night
They make you need more coffee
Naps are always harmful
They reset your body clock to morning
quiz.explanation: Late naps relieve the sleep pressure that helps you fall asleep at bedtime.

cards.title: Wind down before bed, and try a warm bath
cards.body:
Walker recommends an unhurried wind-down before bed, such as reading or gentle music, rather than work or stressful conversations right up to lights-out. One tip he highlights is a warm bath in the evening. It seems backwards, but the bath draws heat to the skin, and your core body temperature then drops afterwards, which is one of the signals that helps bring on sleep.

A regular routine also tells your brain that the day is ending. It doesn't need to be elaborate; it just needs to be consistent.
cards.apply_it: Choose two calming activities for the half hour before bed and do them in the same order each night this week.

quiz.question: Why can a warm bath before bed help sleep, according to Walker?
options: It raises your temperature all night
Core body temperature drops afterwards, which helps signal sleep
It replaces the need for a dark room
It contains melatonin
quiz.explanation: The drop in core temperature after the bath is a cue for sleep.

cards.title: Avoid heavy meals and lots of drinks late at night
cards.body:
Among Walker's practical habits is avoiding large meals and big drinks late in the evening. A heavy meal close to bedtime can cause indigestion that disturbs sleep, and drinking a lot late can wake you to use the bathroom.

This isn't about strict rules, just giving your body time to digest before you lie down. Eating dinner a little earlier and keeping late snacks light is an easy adjustment for many people.
cards.apply_it: Try finishing your evening meal a couple of hours before bed for one week and notice any difference in your nights.

quiz.question: Why does Walker advise against large meals and drinks late at night?
options: Food at night has no effect on sleep
Eating late guarantees deeper sleep
Indigestion and bathroom trips can disturb sleep
Drinking water at night is dangerous
quiz.explanation: Heavy late meals and lots of fluid can interrupt the night.

cards.title: Exercise helps sleep, but not right before bed
cards.body:
Walker encourages regular exercise, around 30 minutes on most days, as a support for good sleep. But he suggests not exercising in the two to three hours before bedtime, since it can leave some people too alert to settle.

The relationship runs both ways: good sleep also improves your energy and motivation to move. If evenings are your only free time, gentler activity such as a walk or stretching may suit better than an intense workout.
cards.apply_it: Schedule your next workout earlier in the day, or swap a late intense session for an evening walk.

quiz.question: What does Walker advise about exercise timing?
options: Exercise only at midnight
Avoid all exercise to sleep better
Exercise right before bed to tire yourself out
Exercise regularly, but not in the two to three hours before bed
quiz.explanation: Regular activity helps, but hard exercise close to bedtime can keep you alert.

cards.title: Watch out for nicotine and medicines that disturb sleep
cards.body:
Walker's sleep tips include avoiding nicotine, a stimulant that can leave smokers sleeping lightly and waking early as cravings return. He also notes that some commonly used medicines, including certain heart, blood-pressure and asthma drugs, and some cough, cold and allergy remedies, can disrupt sleep.

Don't stop a prescribed medicine on your own. If you suspect one is affecting your sleep, ask your doctor or pharmacist whether the timing or type could be adjusted.
cards.apply_it: Check the labels of anything you take in the evening, and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure whether it could affect sleep.

quiz.question: What should you do if you think a prescribed medicine is disturbing your sleep?
options: Ask your doctor or pharmacist about adjusting it
Stop taking it immediately
Double the dose to sleep it off
Ignore it; medicines never affect sleep
quiz.explanation: Some medicines affect sleep, but changes should be made with professional advice.

cards.title: Melatonin tells your body it's night; it doesn't create sleep
cards.body:
Walker explains that melatonin works more like a starting signal than the engine of sleep: it tells the body that night has arrived, while other processes actually generate sleep. That's one reason he is cautious about melatonin supplements for everyday sleeplessness, though they can help reset the body clock, for example with jet lag.

For most people, a more reliable way to support natural melatonin is managing light: dimmer evenings and brighter mornings. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using sleep supplements.
cards.apply_it: Before reaching for a sleep supplement, try two weeks of dimmer evenings and daylight soon after waking.

quiz.question: How does Walker describe melatonin's role?
options: The chemical that produces deep sleep on its own
A timing signal that night has arrived, not the generator of sleep
A stimulant that keeps you awake
A hormone released by caffeine
quiz.explanation: Melatonin signals timing; other processes produce sleep itself.

cards.title: For long-term insomnia, ask about therapy before pills
cards.body:
Walker argues that common sleeping pills tend to sedate rather than produce natural, restorative sleep. He points instead to cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), a structured programme that changes habits and thoughts around sleep, as the better approach for chronic insomnia. Major medical guidelines also recommend CBT-I as the first treatment to try.

If you've struggled with sleep for weeks or months, it's worth asking a doctor about CBT-I. Never stop prescribed medication without medical advice.
cards.apply_it: If poor sleep has lasted more than a few weeks, book a conversation with a doctor and ask specifically about CBT-I.

quiz.question: What approach does Walker favour for chronic insomnia?
options: Stronger sleeping pills
Drinking alcohol before bed
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)
Sleeping only at weekends
quiz.explanation: CBT-I is recommended as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia.

cards.title: Every animal studied sleeps, which shows how essential it is
cards.body:
Walker opens with an evolutionary argument. Sleep appears in every animal species that has been carefully studied, even though sleeping leaves an animal unable to find food, find a mate or watch for predators. If sleep served no vital purpose, he reasons, evolution would likely have got rid of it.

Some creatures have even evolved unusual ways to keep sleeping, such as dolphins resting one half of the brain at a time. The takeaway is a shift in mindset: sleep isn't wasted time to be minimised but a basic biological need.
cards.apply_it: Notice one way you treat sleep as optional, and ask what would change if you saw it as being as essential as food.

quiz.question: What is Walker's evolutionary argument about sleep?
options: Only humans need to sleep
Sleep evolved to waste time
Animals that sleep less live longer
Sleep persists across species despite its risks, so it must be vital
quiz.explanation: Sleep survived evolution despite its dangers, suggesting it serves essential functions.

cards.title: Don't wear sleeplessness as a badge of honour
cards.body:
Walker criticises workplaces and cultures that praise people for working through the night or getting by on little sleep. He cites research suggesting that sleep-deprived employees are less productive and creative, and even more likely to behave unethically, and that tired leaders are rated as less inspiring by their teams.

For managers and anyone building a career, protecting rest is part of doing good work, not a sign of weakness. All-night pushes often cost more in mistakes than they gain in hours.
cards.apply_it: If you lead others, stop sending late-night messages that imply people should be working; schedule them for the morning.

quiz.question: What does the research Walker cites suggest about sleep-deprived workers?
options: They tend to be less productive and creative, and more prone to unethical choices
They are more productive than rested workers
Sleep has no effect on work
They become more inspiring leaders
quiz.explanation: Tiredness was linked to worse performance, ethics and leadership ratings.

cards.title: Sleep and mental health affect each other
cards.body:
Walker highlights that disrupted sleep is common across many mental health conditions, from depression and anxiety to bipolar disorder, and argues that the relationship runs both ways: poor sleep can worsen mood and mental health, and mental health problems can disturb sleep.

Some of his wider claims are debated, but this two-way link is widely accepted. Looking after sleep is one supportive step for mental wellbeing, alongside, not instead of, professional help. If low mood and poor sleep persist, speak to a doctor.
cards.apply_it: Track your mood and your sleep for two weeks; if both are persistently poor, share the record with a doctor.

quiz.question: How does Walker describe the link between sleep and mental health?
options: Sleep has nothing to do with mood
It runs both ways: each can worsen the other
Only mental health affects sleep, not the reverse
Better sleep replaces professional treatment
quiz.explanation: Poor sleep and mental health problems tend to feed into each other.

cards.title: Treat steady sleep as part of a heart-healthy life, without panicking
cards.body:
Walker connects chronic short sleep with higher blood pressure and heart problems. Much of that evidence is observational, so cause and effect are hard to untangle, and critics, including the writer Alexey Guzey, have argued that the book overstates several of its health risks.

Even so, mainstream health bodies now count sufficient, regular sleep as part of a heart-healthy lifestyle, alongside activity, diet and not smoking. The sensible takeaway isn't fear over one bad night, but treating consistent sleep as a long-term habit, like exercise.
cards.apply_it: Add sleep to your health goals this year, with a specific target such as a fixed bedtime on weeknights.

quiz.question: What caution applies to Walker's claims about sleep and heart disease?
options: They are all proven by large trials
Sleep has no link to health
Much of the evidence is observational, and critics say some risks are overstated
One bad night causes heart disease
quiz.explanation: The link is plausible and widely accepted, but the book's specific risks have been challenged.
